theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: The main supply to a small office must be switched off for two hours to change the main board. Who should be told, and when?
options: Only the receptionist, on the morning of the work
Nobody, so that the staff do not complain about it in advance
The manager and staff, in writing, well before the day
The power company only, after the work is finished

questions.stem: Why should an outage notice say which equipment will lose power, such as computers, fridges and the alarm?
options: So people can save work and protect what needs it
So the electrician can charge for each item listed
So the power company can read the notice as well
So the notice looks longer and more official

questions.stem: Two electricians are working on different circuits fed from the same board. How should isolation be managed between them?
options: One padlock is enough for both, held by the senior one
Each tells the other by word of mouth; no locks are used
The first one to finish switches the board back on
Each fits their own lock and removes only their own

questions.stem: Before a newly installed circuit is switched on for the first time, what must the person energising it do?
options: Switch it on quickly while nobody is looking
Confirm that everyone is clear and work is done
Ask the customer to be the one who switches it on
Remove the warning signs one hour beforehand

questions.stem: During a functional check, you are at the board and your partner is at a light fitting in another room, with a radio. Which message is clearest?
options: Okay, I am switching it now, so tell me if anything happens
Switching ON circuit 7, lights Room 4. Confirm when clear
Hold on, I think it might be the next one along
It's on now, I think, can you check something?

questions.stem: On a large site, what is a permit-to-work used for in electrical work?
options: To show that the electrician has paid the site fee
To let any trade switch circuits whenever they need
To replace the need for any locks and tags on isolators
To record who may work on what, under which controls

questions.stem: At the start of a job, a team leader briefs four electricians. Which briefing is best?
options: Tasks, hazards, isolation points and who to report to
A quick "same as yesterday" and then everyone starts
Only the finishing time, so nobody works late
A long talk about past jobs and all of the firm's history

questions.stem: After you explain a two-way (three-way) switching circuit to a trainee, which question best checks that they understood?
options: "Did you understand all of what I just said?"
"That makes sense, doesn't it?"
"Can you show me where the strappers go?"
"Any problems? No? Good."

questions.stem: A customer asks what an RCD does. Which explanation suits her best?
options: It is a residual current device rated at 30 mA IΔn
It detects any imbalance between the line and neutral currents
It is a type of breaker that trips on overloads
It switches off fast if current leaks, to help stop shocks

questions.stem: Your tests show that a customer's old wiring has poor insulation on two circuits. How should you tell her?
options: Tell her it is fine for now, so she is not worried
Explain the risk simply and in writing, with options
Give her the test sheet and leave without explaining
Tell her that everything must be rewired at once

questions.stem: A shop owner is angry that the power was off longer than your notice promised. What should you do first?
options: Listen, apologise and explain what caused the delay
Tell him the delay was the other trades' fault
Ignore him and keep on working so that you finish faster
Tell him he should have read the notice better

questions.stem: Which sentence is best in a test report to a building owner?
options: Circuit 4 is kind of bad, I think, maybe the cable
There are lots of problems everywhere, and it needs loads of work
Circuit 4 (kitchen outlets) fails insulation test; isolated
Everything was tested and some things were not great

questions.stem: A client asks you on site to add four extra outlets that are not in the contract. What should you do?
options: Fit them at once and add the cost at the end
Refuse, because the drawing cannot be changed
Agree the extra work and price in writing first
Fit them free of charge to keep the client happy

questions.stem: The drawings do not show where the main board goes in a new shop. What is the best way to get the answer?
options: Send a written query to the designer through the contractor
Choose a spot yourself and tell nobody until it is fixed
Ask the plumber where he thinks it should go
Wait until the end of the job and see what is left

questions.stem: At a weekly site meeting, why should the electrical team leader bring a short progress list?
options: So the meeting lasts as long as possible
To report progress, problems and needs clearly
So the other trades cannot raise any of their issues
To avoid having to speak at the meeting

questions.stem: When a new installation is handed over, what should the customer receive and be shown?
options: Only the invoice, showing the full total to pay
A spare key to the electrician's van
A list of the other jobs the firm has done nearby
Test results, board chart and how to test the RCD

questions.stem: In a noisy plant room with machines running, what is the best way to give a short instruction?
options: Move somewhere quieter, then check back
Shout the instruction once across the room
Send a long text message and hope it is read
Say it quickly and walk away

questions.stem: A new electrician on your team is deaf in one ear. How should you adjust your briefings?
options: Leave them out of briefings to save time
Speak louder only to them, in front of everyone
Give them the easiest jobs so they need no briefing
Ask what helps, face them, and write key points

questions.stem: A supplier phones to say the 6 mm² cable is out of stock and offers 4 mm² instead. What should you do?
options: Accept it, since it is cheaper and lighter
Not without the designer's written approval
Accept it and fit it on the shortest runs
Accept it, as all cable is rated the same

questions.stem: A board is isolated for work and must stay that way overnight. What written warning should be on it?
options: A handwritten sign saying "Back in five minutes"
A note telling people where to find the spare keys
A danger tag with name, date and reason
No sign, so that people do not worry

questions.stem: A team leader leaves a written note for a trainee about tomorrow's work. Which note is clearest?
options: Do all of the outlets in the usual way, as you normally would
Fix boxes etc. where needed and wire up
Sort out room 3 when you can
Fix four outlet boxes in Room 3, 300 mm above FFL

questions.stem: Before installing a new inverter, which document gives its wiring, clearances and safety warnings?
options: The supplier's delivery note
The firm's price list
The maker's installation manual
The customer's electricity bill

questions.stem: A trainee tells you a breaker in a client's board is hot and smells of burning. What should you do?
options: Thank them, make it safe and report it to the client
Tell them to stop worrying about other people's boards

Spray it with water to cool it down

questions.stem: A trainee has wired a board neatly but left two terminals loose. Which feedback is best?
options: "This is all wrong, do it again."
"Neat layout, but two terminals are loose; check all."
"Looks fine to me, carry on."
"I will fix it myself; you go and sweep the floor instead."

questions.stem: The electrical inspector lists three defects in your team's work. What is the best response?
options: Argue each point until the inspector gives up
Note each one, ask about anything unclear, fix them
Tell the client the inspector is being unfair
Ignore the list and book another inspection with someone else

questions.stem: A plumber keeps moving your cable drums to reach his pipes, and tempers are rising. What is the best first step?
options: Talk calmly and agree where things go
Move his pipes out of the way in return
Complain about him to the client
Hide the drums so that he cannot touch them

questions.stem: A neighbour asks you what alarm system and safe a client has had wired in. What should you say?
options: Tell them, as long as they seem friendly
Tell them only about the alarm, but not about the safe
Show them the job drawings stored on your phone
Politely say you cannot discuss a client's job

questions.stem: Why should a site diary note the time each circuit was switched off and on?
options: To show the client how hard the team works
To record how long the tea breaks lasted
To give a clear record if a problem or claim arises
To help the team remember their lunch order

questions.stem: Which is the best way to show a client where new outlets will go in a house she lives in?
options: Describe it in words over the phone only
Send a long email about it with no drawing attached
Walk through with a marked plan and tape marks on walls

questions.stem: A worker receives an electric shock and collapses. Once the supply is off, what should be communicated first?
options: A message to the client about the delay
A text to the supplier for more cable
A note in the site diary for later
A call for emergency help, with the exact location

questions.stem: Why should radio messages during switching be short and use agreed words?
options: So the batteries in the radios last longer
So there is no doubt about what is being switched
So others on the same channel cannot understand them
So the messages can be sent faster than talking

questions.stem: Before a government electrical inspector visits, what should the team leader prepare?
options: Test results, drawings and access to the work
A long speech about how good the team is
A gift to make the inspector feel welcome
Nothing; the inspector will find everything

questions.stem: During other work, you find that the earth rod connection at a house is badly corroded. How should you report it?
options: Tell the owner and write it on your report
Say nothing, as it was not part of your job
Fix it without telling anyone or charging
Tell the neighbour so they can pass it on

questions.stem: You must show two trainees how to terminate armoured cable. Which order works best?
options: Let them try first, then explain what went wrong
Explain, show, let them try, then check and correct
Hand them the manual and leave them to it
Do it yourself quickly while they watch from afar

questions.stem: A supervisor tells you by phone to "just bypass" a faulty RCD to get a shop working. What should you do?
options: Do it, since the supervisor is in charge
Do it, but only until the end of the working day
Refuse politely, explain the danger and report it
Do it and tell the customer not to worry

questions.stem: A client wants a quotation for a solar system. Which message is best to confirm the site visit?
options: "We will be there sometime next week, probably."
"I will call you later to sort out a good day."
"We will visit soon to have a look at the roof."
"Tuesday, 9 a.m., about 1 hour; we need roof access."

questions.stem: At a site meeting, the builder's plan would put a water tank directly above your main board. What should you do?
options: Stay quiet and move the board later on your own
Agree to it, since the builder runs the meeting
Leave the meeting to call the client at once
Raise it, explain the risk, and get it recorded

questions.stem: A job card says "Replace 3 lamps in corridor", but you find a burnt lamp holder causing the failures. What should you do?
options: Replace the lamps only, as the job card says
Leave without doing anything, as the card is wrong
Make safe, tell the client, agree the extra work
Replace the holder quietly and charge double

questions.stem: A visiting engineer who speaks mainly Spanish has little English. What will help most?
options: Short sentences, drawings and checking back often
Speaking much faster to get the meeting over
Using as much trade slang as possible
Leaving all the talking to someone else

questions.stem: You send photos of a damaged board to your supervisor by phone. What makes them most useful?
options: Taking them quickly from far away
Clear close-ups, with location and circuit
Adding funny filters so they stand out
Sending them to the team's social media page

questions.stem: You must hand over a half-finished board change to another electrician tomorrow. Which handover is safest?
options: Tell them it is mostly done and they will see
Walk through it, with a written note of what is live
Leave the board cover off so they can see how far you got

questions.stem: When you explain a fault to a worried homeowner, which body language helps?
options: Arms folded and looking at your phone
Standing very close and talking loudly
Looking at the floor and mumbling
Calm voice, eye contact and an open stance

questions.stem: Which is the best wording for a sign on the door of a switch room?
options: Keep out or else!!!

Danger: electrical. Authorised staff only

questions.stem: A trainee almost drilled into a hidden cable but stopped in time. Why should this near miss be reported?
options: So the cause can be fixed before someone is hurt
So the trainee can be punished for the mistake
So that the client pays extra for all of the lost time
So the report file looks fuller at the audit

questions.stem: You emailed a client about a safety defect, but she has not replied in a week. What should you do?
options: Forget it, since you have already told her once
Follow up by phone and record that you did so
Switch off her supply without telling her

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the name of the short safety talk given to a team at the start of a job or a shift?
What do we call a change to the agreed work, such as extra outlets, that is priced and agreed separately?
What is the name of the label fixed with a lock to an isolator, giving the worker's name, the date and the reason?
What do the letters O&M stand for in the O&M manual handed to a client?
What word, often used on a radio, means "I have received and understood your message"?
What is the name of the daily written record on site of work done, visitors, weather and problems?
What do the letters ETA stand for in a supplier's text such as "Delivery ETA 2 p.m."?
When spelling a circuit label over a radio with the phonetic alphabet, which word stands for the letter B?
What do we call the notice telling building users that the power will be off for a set time?
In an email, which address box sends a copy without the other receivers seeing that address?
What is the name of the written request for payment sent to a client after the work is done?
Which letters name the tax on sales that is added to quotations and invoices in Jamaica?
What do we call the written step-by-step procedure that tells everyone how to switch off, lock off and prove a piece of equipment dead?
What word describes information that must not be shared outside the job, such as a client's alarm codes?
What do we call the list, agreed with the client at the end of a job, of items that are not finished or need fixing?

essays.stem: The power to a busy medical office must be off for three hours on a Saturday so the main board can be replaced. Explain how you would plan and communicate the outage.
essays.modelAnswer: First I agree the date and time with the office manager, choosing a time with the least effect on patients. I ask what equipment needs power: fridges for medicines, computers, the alarm, phones and any medical equipment, so they can plan, for example moving medicines to another fridge or using a generator set up by a competent person. I give a written outage notice well in advance, at least several days, saying the date, start and finish times, what will be off, what staff should do before (save work, shut down computers), and a contact name and number. I tell the alarm company if needed. The day before, I confirm by phone that it is still going ahead. On the day, I tell the manager when the power goes off and when it is back, and ask them to check their equipment. If the work runs late, I tell them at once with a new time. I record the times in the site diary.
markingPoints: Agrees a suitable time with the manager
Finds out critical equipment and plans for it
Written notice in good time with dates, times, effects, actions and contact
Confirms the day before and updates on the day, including delays
Tells others affected (alarm company) and records times

essays.stem: Your team of four will replace a distribution board in a factory. Describe the briefing you would give before work starts, and how you would manage communication when the new board is switched on.
essays.modelAnswer: I would brief the team at the work area with the drawings and the method statement. I explain the job and give each person a clear task. I point out the hazards: live parts nearby, the supply side of the isolator, sharp edges and lifting. I show the isolation point, and explain that each person fits their own lock and tag and removes only their own, and that we prove dead with a tester checked before and after. I agree how we will talk to each other: who is in charge, and which radio channel or words to use. I ask each person to tell me back their task and the isolation points, and I invite questions. At switch-on, only I give the order. I check all work is finished, covers are on and tools are out. I confirm by name that every person is clear and has removed their lock. Then I announce "Switching on main board now", switch on, and we check each circuit in turn.
markingPoints: Clear tasks and hazards explained at the work area
Isolation: personal locks and tags, prove dead with a checked tester
Agreed communication method and one person in charge
Checks understanding by asking team to repeat back
Switch-on: work complete, everyone clear and locks off, announced

essays.stem: Your tests on an older house show a missing earth on two circuits and no RCD. Explain how you would tell the owner, who is not technical, and confirm it in writing.
essays.modelAnswer: I would sit down with the owner and explain in plain words, without jargon. I would say that the earth wire is like a safety path that carries current away if something goes wrong, and that two circuits do not have one, so a fault could make metal parts live and give someone a shock. I would explain that an RCD is a device that switches off very fast if current leaks, and that the house does not have one. I would say how serious this is and what I recommend: putting in the missing earths and fitting RCD protection, and I would give a price or say I will send a quotation. I would answer questions and check that the owner understood, without frightening them or pressuring them. Then I would send a short written report the same day, listing the findings, the risks and the recommendations, attach the test results, and keep a copy with a note that we talked.
markingPoints: Plain words, no jargon
Explains the earth and RCD and the risk clearly
Gives recommendations and price or quotation
Checks understanding and answers questions without pressure
Confirms in a written report with test results, copy kept

essays.stem: Explain why agreed radio procedures matter when two people carry out switching and functional checks in different parts of a building. Give an example of a good exchange.
essays.modelAnswer: When two people are out of sight of each other, a misunderstanding can lead to a circuit being switched on while someone is still working on it, or the wrong circuit being switched. Agreed procedures make every message clear. Each message should name who is calling, say exactly which circuit and what action, and wait for a reply. The receiver repeats the key part back. Nothing is switched until the reply is heard. Short, agreed words avoid confusion, and the radios are checked before starting. An example: "Kemar, this is Tanya at the board. Ready to switch ON circuit 7, Room 4 lights. Are you clear?" Kemar replies: "Tanya, Kemar. Circuit 7, Room 4 lights. I am clear. Go ahead." Tanya switches on and says: "Circuit 7 is ON." Kemar confirms: "Circuit 7 ON, lights working." If there is no reply, Tanya does not switch.
markingPoints: Explains the risk of misunderstanding when out of sight
Messages name the caller, circuit and action
Receiver repeats back; no action without a reply
Short agreed words and radios checked
Gives a clear example exchange

essays.stem: A shop owner asks you to bypass an RCD that keeps tripping, so his freezers stay on. Explain how you would respond and what you would do.
essays.modelAnswer: I would stay calm and polite, and say clearly that I cannot bypass the RCD. I would explain in plain words that it is tripping because current is leaking somewhere, and that the RCD is the thing that stops someone getting a dangerous shock. Bypassing it would leave the fault there with no protection. I would then offer help: I can find the fault, for example by unplugging the equipment one item at a time and testing the circuits, so the freezers can run safely. If one freezer is faulty, I can suggest moving its contents and having it repaired. If the owner still insists, I would not do it, and I would explain that it would be unsafe and against my duty. I would write down what was found and said, give the owner a written note, and report it to my supervisor so there is a record.
markingPoints: Calm, polite and clear refusal
Explains why in plain words (leakage and shock protection)
Offers a safe solution such as finding the fault
Does not give in to pressure
Records the conversation, gives a written note and reports it

essays.stem: The air-conditioning installer and your team both need the same ceiling space this week, and the job is falling behind. Describe how you would sort this out.
essays.modelAnswer: I would first talk to the air-conditioning team leader in person, calmly and early, rather than let the problem grow. I would listen to their needs and explain ours, using the drawings to show where our cables and their ducts and pipes go. Together we would look for a fair plan, for example one team working in the ceiling in the morning and the other in the afternoon, or one area at a time, and agree who goes first where one route must be in before the other. We would agree how to keep each other informed, such as a quick check each morning. If we could not agree, or if routes clash on the drawings, I would take it to the site manager to decide, with the facts. I would write the agreement in the site diary and tell my team, so everyone works to the same plan, and raise it at the next site meeting if it affects the programme.
markingPoints: Talks early and calmly in person
Listens, explains needs and uses the drawings
Agrees a fair plan (times, areas, order)
Escalates to the site manager if no agreement
Records the agreement and tells the team

essays.stem: A trainee drilled into a hidden cable, which tripped the breaker; nobody was hurt. Describe what your written incident report should contain.
essays.modelAnswer: The report should give the date, time and exact place of the incident, and the names of the people involved and any witnesses. It should describe what happened in order, using facts, not opinions or blame: for example, "At 10:15 the trainee was drilling a 25 mm hole at 1.2 m height in the east wall of Room 3. The bit struck a cable in the wall and the circuit 5 breaker tripped." It should say what was done straight away: the drill was put down, the circuit was isolated, locked off and proved dead, and the trainee was checked for injury. It should record the damage, such as the cable and the drill, and say they were taken out of use. It should give the likely causes, such as no detector used or the cable not in the expected route, and the actions to stop it happening again, with names and dates. It ends with the writer's name, signature and the date it was written.
markingPoints: Date, time, place, people and witnesses
Factual account in order, without blame
Immediate actions taken, including isolation and checks
Damage recorded and equipment withdrawn
Causes, actions with names and dates, signed and dated

essays.stem: Describe how you would hand over a newly wired small restaurant to its owner at the end of the job.
essays.modelAnswer: I would agree a time with the owner and walk round the building together. I would show where the main switch and distribution board are, how to read the circuit chart, how to switch off a circuit safely, and how to test the RCDs with the test button and how often to do it. I would show any special items, such as the extractor fan controls or timers. I would hand over the documents: the test results and certificate, the as-built drawings, the circuit chart, and the makers' instructions and warranties, ideally in an O&M file. Any items not yet finished would be listed on a snag list with dates to fix them, agreed with the owner. I would explain what to do if a breaker trips and who to call. I would ask if they have questions and check they understood. Finally, I would ask the owner to sign to say the handover was done, and keep a copy.
markingPoints: Walk-round with the owner
Shows main switch, board, chart and RCD testing
Hands over test results, drawings and makers' documents
Agrees a snag list with dates
Checks understanding and gets a signed handover

essays.stem: Your team includes an experienced electrician who reads little, a trainee who is shy about asking questions, and a worker whose first language is Spanish. Explain how you would make sure all of them understand your instructions.
essays.modelAnswer: I would use more than one way of passing on each instruction. For the electrician who reads little, I would explain face to face and show on the drawing or on the job, without embarrassing him in front of others, and use pictures and marked drawings rather than long written notes. For the shy trainee, I would ask open questions, such as "Show me how you will connect this", rather than "Do you understand?", and make time to talk one-to-one, so they feel safe to ask. For the Spanish-speaking worker, I would use short, simple sentences, speak clearly, use drawings and gestures, and check back. Someone who speaks both languages could help, and key safety words could be agreed. With everyone, I would ask them to tell me back the main points, watch the first part of the work, and treat everyone with respect, so they are comfortable coming to me with problems.
markingPoints: Uses several methods: spoken, shown, drawn
Supports the reader without embarrassment
Encourages the shy trainee with open questions and one-to-one time
Plain language, drawings and checking back for the second-language speaker
Checks understanding of all and shows respect

essays.stem: On a job, the client's representative asks for several changes on site by word of mouth. Explain why this can cause problems and how you would make sure changes are properly agreed and recorded.
essays.modelAnswer: Changes agreed only by word of mouth can be forgotten or remembered differently. The person asking may not have the authority to approve extra cost. The change may not match the design or the rules, other trades may not know about it, and there may be arguments about payment later. When a change is asked for, I would thank the person and explain that it must be confirmed in writing before we do it. I would note exactly what is wanted, check it with my supervisor and the designer if it affects the design, and work out the cost and time. Then I would send a written variation for the client to approve and sign. Only after approval would the team do the work. I would record the change in the site diary, mark it on the drawings for the as-built record, and mention it at the next site meeting so everyone knows.
markingPoints: Explains the risks: forgotten, no authority, design or rule problems, payment disputes
Asks for written confirmation before acting
Checks with supervisor or designer; works out cost and time
Written variation approved before work starts
Records in diary and drawings; shares at site meeting

practical1.title: Plan a power outage, brief the team and role-play the switching
practical1.brief: The assessor gives the group a scenario: the main board in a small office must be changed, with power off for three hours. As a group: (1) write an outage notice and a short email to the office manager; (2) prepare a one-page briefing sheet with tasks, hazards, isolation points and communication rules; (3) one member gives the briefing to the rest, who repeat back their tasks; (4) role-play the isolation and switch-on on a training board that is NOT connected to any supply, using personal locks and tags and agreed radio or spoken messages between two members out of sight of each other. Members swap roles so that each person writes, speaks and acts in at least one part. Finish with a short written debrief: what worked and what to improve.
materials: Paper, pens and a computer or phone for the email
Training board not connected to any supply, with a lock-off kit, personal padlocks and tags
Two-way radios or phones for the role play
Briefing sheet template and debrief form
photos: The email to the office manager on screen
The briefing being given, with team members repeating back
Personal locks and tags fitted on the training board
The switching role play with the two members in different places
checklist: Wrote clearly and correctly in at least one document
Included dates, times, effects, actions and a contact in the notice
Gave or took part in the briefing and repeated back their task correctly
Fitted and removed only their own lock and tag
Used clear, agreed messages and waited for confirmation
Listened and responded to others with respect
safety: The training board is never connected to a supply in this task
Treat the role play as real: no shortcuts with locks and tags
Keep walkways clear while moving between rooms
Follow the assessor's instructions at all times

practical2.title: Explain test results to a client and handle a request for unsafe work
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the group a set of test results for a small shop, with three defects (for example a low insulation reading, a missing RCD and a damaged outlet). As a group: (1) write a short plain-language report for the owner, with the findings, risks and recommendations; (2) draw up a snag list and a written variation for one extra item the owner asks for; (3) role-play a meeting in which one member explains the results to the "owner" (played by the assessor or a member), checks understanding and answers questions; (4) role-play the owner asking the electrician to bypass the RCD, and refuse politely with reasons and a safe alternative; (5) write a follow-up email confirming what was agreed. Members swap roles so each person writes one item and speaks in one role play.
materials: Test results and scenario from the assessor
Report, snag list and variation templates
Paper, pens, and a computer or phone
A camera or phone to photograph the role plays
photos: The snag list and the variation form
The group's notes from each role play
checklist: Wrote findings in plain words, with risks and recommendations
Used facts and figures correctly from the test results
Explained clearly, without jargon, and checked the listener understood
Refused the unsafe request politely and offered a safe alternative
Listened, showed respect and used good body language
Took part in writing and in at least one role play
safety: No electrical equipment is used in this task
Keep role plays respectful; no shouting or physical contact
Keep client details in the scenario private
Follow the assessor's instructions at all times
